lead: A multimedia system is not one program; it is a stack of stages joined by a common clock. It captures sound and pictures, compresses each stream, buffers the result, stores or sends it, and finally plays it out. The design exists because audio and video are continuous: they must arrive at a fixed rate. A phone video call, an online class recording and a railway safety video all use this pipeline. This chapter names the layers and shows where timing is protected.
prereq: You need Unit 4 (media types and compression basics); network timing appears later in 6.5.

blocks.text: Text and a still image are non-temporal. The system may show a page in 10 ms or in 10 s; nothing breaks. Audio, video and animation are temporal, also called continuous media. A video has a frame rate, for example 30 frames per second. A frame shown late is a glitch; a frame lost is a gap. Audio has a sample rate, for example 44,100 samples per second. Samples must be played at that rate. A clock drives presentation, not the user's click.

The architecture is layered because each job is different. Capture makes a digital stream from a microphone, camera or file. The codec reduces bits. The buffer and synchronisation unit holds short bursts and aligns audio with video. Storage and the file system keep blocks on disk. Network delivery sends packets. Presentation plays out to screen and speaker. The buffer stage is special: it is where timing is repaired rather than merely carried.
The same six stages appear in a phone, a set-top box and a classroom PC. Their hardware changes; the contracts between stages do not. That is why the model is called general purpose.

items: Capture converts light or sound into numbers: pixel values, PCM samples or a compressed file read from storage.
The codec stage compresses each media type separately. A video codec and an audio codec may run on the same chip, but they produce separate streams.
The buffer and synchronisation stage stores a small playout buffer. It absorbs jitter and inserts or drops timing so that audio and video share one timeline.
The file system stores media in blocks and uses read-ahead so that a disk can supply a continuous stream without long waits.
The network interface packetises the stream for delivery. It may mark packets for quality of service, as covered in 6.5.
The presentation layer decodes, renders and plays out frames and samples at the rate the user expects.

blocks.text: R = W × H × d × f + f_s × b_s × c
blocks.where: R is the raw bit rate in bit/s; W and H are frame width and height in pixels; d is bits per pixel; f is frames per second; f_s is audio samples per second; b_s is bits per sample; c is the number of audio channels. Compression and packet overhead are not included.

blocks.text: The formula shows why multimedia stresses a system. A modest frame size at a common colour depth already produces hundreds of megabits per second if left raw. Compression exists to bring R down to what storage and networks can carry.

USB is a device and data interface. A webcam sends frames over USB; a microphone sends PCM samples; the same cable supplies power. HDMI is a display and data interface. It carries uncompressed video with embedded audio from a set-top box or laptop to a screen. HDMI is a live link, not a file system.

A phone is built for low power, so it uses hardware codecs and small buffers. A set-top box is fixed-function and expects a steady transport stream. A classroom PC is flexible but not real-time by default; its operating system may delay a software codec. Those differences sit inside the same six-layer model.

figure.caption: The buffer and synchronisation box is the one that gives continuous media their timing; every other layer feeds or drains it.

examples.question: A video is 640 × 480 pixels, 24 bits per pixel, at 30 frames per second, with stereo audio at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits per sample. Find the raw video bit rate, the audio bit rate, the total bit rate and the storage for a 2-minute clip. Use 1 GB = 10^9 bytes.
steps: List the data: W = 640 pixels, H = 480 pixels, d = 24 bit/pixel, f = 30 frame/s, f_s = 44,100 sample/s, b_s = 16 bit/sample, c = 2 channels, t = 120 s.
Video bits per frame = W × H × d = 640 × 480 × 24 = 7,372,800 bit/frame.
Audio bit rate = f_s × b_s × c = 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bit/s = 1.4112 Mbit/s.
examples.answer: The raw total bit rate is 222,595,200 bit/s, about 222.6 Mbit/s, and the 2-minute clip needs 3,338,928,000 bytes, about 3.34 GB, before compression.
examples.check:
W = 640
H = 480
d = 24
f = 30
f_s = 44100
b_s = 16
c = 2
t = 120
video = W * H * d * f
audio = f_s * b_s * c
total = video + audio
storage_bytes = total * t // 8
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(video)
    print(audio)
    print(total)
    print(storage_bytes)

traps: Forgetting that audio adds its own bit rate. A video-only answer misses 1,411,200 bit/s in the worked example.
Mixing bits with bytes. 640 × 480 × 24 is bits per frame, not bytes; divide by 8 only when bytes are asked.
Multiplying sample rate by frame rate. Audio and video have independent clocks and independent bit rates.
Treating a buffer as compression. A buffer absorbs jitter and aligns streams; it does not reduce the number of bits.
Confusing Mbit/s with MB/s. A rate of 222.6 Mbit/s is about 27.8 MB/s, not 222.6 MB/s.

quiz.q: What is a temporal medium? Give two examples.
quiz.a: A temporal medium must be presented at a fixed rate or its meaning and quality break. Examples: digital audio and digital video.

quiz.q: Why does a multimedia architecture need a buffer and synchronisation stage?
quiz.a: It absorbs short timing variations from storage or the network. It also aligns separate audio and video streams onto one presentation timeline, so a late packet does not immediately become a lost frame.

quiz.q: A 320 × 240 video uses 24 bit/pixel at 30 frame/s. Mono audio is 48,000 sample/s at 16 bit/sample. Find the total raw bit rate.
A phone and a set-top box both play video. Name one architectural difference forced by their use.
quiz.a: The phone must save power, so it relies on hardware codecs and small buffers. The set-top box expects a steady transport stream and sends uncompressed output over HDMI to a TV.

quiz.q: Name one job of USB and one job of HDMI in a multimedia system.
quiz.a: USB carries data from a camera or microphone and can supply power. HDMI carries uncompressed video and embedded audio to a display.

quiz.q: Why is a still image called non-temporal even if it is a large file?
quiz.a: Its display has no fixed playout rate. The system can load and show it at any speed without breaking a timeline; file size affects delay, not timing.

quiz.q: If audio is 1,411,200 bit/s and the total is 222,595,200 bit/s, what percentage of the total is audio?
Why can one six-layer model describe a classroom PC and a phone, and what changes between them?
quiz.a: The stages keep the same contracts: capture, compress, buffer, store or send, and present. What changes is implementation: hardware versus software codecs, buffer size, power budget, and the physical delivery link.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems split these layers across chips and processes: camera pipelines on a phone, hardware decoders in a TV, and software media frameworks on a PC. Streaming products add adaptive segment selection and clock recovery on top of the buffer stage. Search for media pipeline architecture, jitter buffer, and HDMI audio embedding to see the same ideas in industry form.
